articles.title: Apple Launches Apple Upgrade: Here’s How the New iPhone, Apple Watch, Mac, and iPad Lease Program Works
articles.subtitle: Apple has introduced a new program aimed at making an upgrade to the company’s latest products a bit more manageable for price-conscious customers. The company is calling the program Apple Upgrade and it replaces the previous iPhone Upgrade Program.
articles.author: OWC Rocket Yard
articles.content:
Apple has introduced a new program aimed at making an upgrade to the company’s latest products a bit more manageable for price-conscious customers. The company is calling the program Apple Upgrade and it replaces the previous iPhone Upgrade Program.

And while Apple Upgrade is designed to deliver new Apple products at reasonable monthly payments, it works a bit differently than the previous upgrade program or Apple’s current Apple Card Monthly Installments. That’s because it’s a lease program built in partnership with Klarna. Apple Upgrade is live in the Apple Store now, so let’s talk about how it works so you’ll know if the new program makes sense for you.

How Apple Upgrade Works

Because Apple Upgrade is a lease program, it works similarly to a car lease in that you are not financing a purchase. Instead, because Apple is running the program through Klarna, Klarna is the owner of any device you lease through the program and you pay a set monthly payment to lease the device from them.

Apple is offering lease terms of 12 or 24 months for iPhone and Apple Watch. For Mac and iPad leases, the program offers 24- or 36-month terms. You’ll have to enroll in the program to use it which requires being approved through a soft credit check that Apple says won’t affect your credit score.

Once approved, you’ll pick your device and pay a monthly payment for that device until the end of your lease. Apple says leasing prices start as low as $17.99 per month for iPhone, $11.99 for Apple Watch, $24.99 for Mac, and $11.99 for iPad. At the end of your lease you have a decision to make: pay to purchase the device or send it back to Apple. One crucial detail for those worried about predatory lending practices, Apple is not including interest in its lease calculations.

And if you’re wondering why the monthly payments Apple is offering through Apple Upgrade are lower than what a no-interest financing plan would offer for the same device, that’s because these payments are calculated differently. Depending on the lease term you agree to, the program starts by essentially guessing what the value of your device will be at the end of your lease to calculate the residual value of your device.

Once they have an estimated residual value, they subtract that residual from the total purchase price and then divide that figure by however many months your lease term spans. So the lease payments are lower than financing because you’re dividing a lower figure than the total purchase price.

Let’s take a look at the Apple Upgrade pricing for an iPhone 17 Pro Max with 256GB of storage to see how this works.

An Example Lease Through Apple Upgrade

iPhone 17 Pro Max 256GB: $1,199 purchase price $1,199 – $359.24 (estimated residual value after 24 months) = $839.76 (This is the fiigure the program divides by the total number of payments you’ll make over the lease term.) $839.76 / 24 = $34.99 per month.

In this example, you would lease the iPhone 17 Pro Max by making payments of $34.99 per month for 24 months. Once your lease is up, you’ll be able to pay an estimated $359.24 to purchase the phone and cover its residual value. Or you can ship the device back to Apple and buy or lease a new iPhone.

Other Things to be Aware Of

Apple does allow you to combine a trade-in with Apple Upgrade to lower your monthly payment even further. Plus, if you use your Apple Card to pay your lease, you do get 3% cash back on those payments.

Another crucial detail is that the payment program is handled through the Klarna app rather than the Apple Store app.

And while you can add AppleCare+ or AppleCare One to a device leased through Apple Upgrade, AppleCare is not included with your lease.

Finally, keeping up with your lease term dates is important. If you do nothing at the end of your lease, the lease automatically converts to a month-to-month arrangement for up to six months, and your payment may increase during that stretch.

articles.title: Pastebot 3 Doubles Down on Mac Clipboard Automation and Introduces Two New Business Models
articles.subtitle: Pastebot’s Quick Menu. Tapbots has released Pastebot 3, a ground-up rewrite of the Mac clipboard manager that includes several powerful automation and customization options, along with two new pricing models.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Pastebot’s Quick Menu.

Tapbots has released Pastebot 3, a ground-up rewrite of the Mac clipboard manager that includes several powerful automation and customization options, along with two new pricing models.

Pastebot was already one of the Mac’s best clipboard utilities, capable of managing an extensive collection of copied text and images in multiple formats, PDFs, URLs, files, and HTML, along with metadata. The app can handle up to 1,500 clippings and features fast search, extensive customizable keyboard shortcuts, list and detail views of clipboard items, and iCloud sync between multiple Macs.

Pastebot 3’s main menu.

What sets Pastebot 3 apart is its addition of deep automation tools. Not only does the update add MCP support, making it an excellent tool to use with Claude or ChatGPT/Codex, but it includes a brand new CLI that you or an agent can use from Terminal or incorporate into scripts you build. Commands include:

List available Pastebins

Browse and search clipboard history

Filter results by Pastebin or date

Retrieve the full text of a clipping

Retrieve images from clippings

List available Pastebot filters

Apply filters to clippings or supplied text

Place an existing clipping on the clipboard

Create new text or image clippings

Paste clipboard contents into the frontmost app

Delete individual clippings

Clear the main clipboard history

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: Splatoon Raiders: The Kotaku Review
articles.subtitle: Nintendo Splatoon splatoon raiders Man, guys, Splatoon is over a decade old? It’s kind of nuts that in that time we’ve gotten three main entries, plus now a new single-player-centric variation on the theme in Splatoon Raiders.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Nintendo Splatoon splatoon raiders

Man, guys, Splatoon is over a decade old? It’s kind of nuts that in that time we’ve gotten three main entries, plus now a new single-player-centric variation on the theme in Splatoon Raiders. Nintendo has been rightfully praised for its interpretation of the competitive shooter, a genre that if you had asked me ahead of Splatoon ’s announcement, I would have said Nintendo cannot and will not ever play in.

But it has, and been riotously successful with it. While the main three Splatoon games had single-player campaigns, Splatoon Raiders is Nintendo’s first proper attempt to take a stab at what a meaty, mission-based shooter looks like.

If you’ve ever played a Splatoon, you’re probably not that worried about how well it’s going to translate. You certainly shouldn’t be.

Splatoon Raiders sends a trio of treasure hunters (who moonlight as a band) and their pilot-turned-mechanic out to a set of deserted islands said to be full of sick loot.

These islands are also full of Salmonids, a group of sapient life forms that exist in the same world as Splatoon ’s Octolings and Inklings but who, for some reason, are not treated as reasoning beings and are instead largely shot on sight with ink guns that kill them. Look, this is a goofy and lighthearted Nintendo game, and the dev team clearly just regards the Salmonids as thoughtless monsters.

But it is a little weird to give them a clearly expansive culture with art and music and society, publish a dev interview about how internally everyone felt bad about murdering them, and then commit to it anyway. I was sort of hoping for at least an attempt at a better explanation for recreational colonialism than Splatoon Raiders gave me.

It may just generally be folly to expect more from a Splatoon story, even a single-player one. The actual plot, when you’re not inking Salmonids to death, is fine. Cute, even. Shiver, Frye, and Big Man are fun, if shallow, companions on the islands, and as unimpressed as I was with the overall depth of what was going on here, their big, joyful personalities are a key part of what makes Splatoon Raiders ’ finale so triumphant and effective.

There’s also loads here, buried in hidden collectible scrolls, for Splatoon lore nerds to feast on. I didn’t understand how it all connects, but I’m sure whoever the Splatoon lore YouTubers are, they’ll catch me up later. But while I’m willing to praise what Splatoon Raiders added to our greater understanding of the Splatoon world, I wish there was more aesthetic variety in the maps you visit.

I don’t really feel like I’m hanging out in a lived-in world so much as a series of sandy beaches, a glacier, a volcano, a cave, and a temple. That’s it, and those same styles are repeated ad nauseum across some 50 stages.

Speaking of aesthetics, I wish Splatoon Raiders had more and better fashion options, and better music. I think the developers offered a great explanation for why the soundtrack is basically a bunch of people banging pots and pans together, but I still didn’t enjoy most of it (the final boss theme rips). These two issues I found particularly surprising given how critical both fashion and music have been to the Splatoon universe over the years.

But all this is incidental to the experience of actually playing Splatoon Raiders, which is a blast. Splatoon ’s single-player modes have always been great, and Splatoon Raiders lets that greatness loose.

The campaigns of yore have traditionally been very obstacle-course heavy, and those are present here, too, in all their glory (and terror; some of them are very difficult), but they exist alongside a variety of other missions including objective-based adventures, those where you fight through waves of enemies on a time limit, and big open spaces where you run around and shoot guys until you fill up a meter.

There are small boss battles and big ones, too, and stages that throw increasingly obnoxious combinations of familiar enemies at you that make you go “Oh no” to yourself when you see what’s in front of you. If I see one of those pot lid snipers aiming at me, I am dropping everything to go ruin its day before it ruins mine. It’s very effective enemy design!

Which, speaking of, I love every weird little dude in this game. Splatoon Raiders is full of incredible little details, like the bits and bobs of human trash all the characters use for armor and weapons. Why is my ink gun a dish soap bottle? It’s amazing.

As I played, I thought a lot about how “cover” is a pretty typical thing to find in shooters. You’re often meant to hide behind things and shoot out from them. Splatoon ’s multiplayer trilogy discourages this, but still has lots of vertical obstacles you can hide behind, climb up, and use to your advantage. Splatoon Raiders throws out the idea entirely.

Most of its levels are flat, or at worst sloped, and waves of enemies pile on top of you like a gaggle of exuberant children at 6am on Christmas. Theoretically, you can make your own cover by spraying ink, but enemies can still see and hit you while you swim. A few of them (like those annoying snipers sitting on towers of pot lids) can shoot through walls for some reason and hit you even if you do hide.

Splatoon Raiders wants you in the middle of the action as much as possible.

articles.title: App report: Kicking my World Cup withdrawal
articles.subtitle: (Left to right): Annotate, Kickabout, and Undolly. For the most part, I’m going to focus on Mac apps with these columns, because that’s where the action seems to be these days.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
For the most part, I’m going to focus on Mac apps with these columns, because that’s where the action seems to be these days. But iOS remains a vibrant platform, too, and every now and again, we’ll look at some of the interesting apps being created for iPhones and iPads. This is one of those now and agains.

Want to see your app included in a future round-up? Get in touch at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief description of your app, and you just might make the cut.

Kickabout

The World Cup is just a memory now, but if you’re missing the daily infusion of soccer (or football, depending on what part of the globe you’re reading this from), Kickabout brings the action back to your iOS device in a very condensed form.

Kickabout will be immediately familiar to anyone who’s ever gathered around a foosball table in a rec room, with a look that will bring a smile to the face of Subbuteo tabletop football aficionados. You take charge of an 8-player team, with players only free to move about certain areas of the pitch. (No length-of-the-field Maradona-esque wonder golazos for your squad.

) You use your finger to drag your players around, swiping any which way to boot the ball toward the goal as you look to rack up the most goals in each 2-minute match.

Goals and shots off the post earn you points, which translates to tickets that you cash in to collect various national teams, from the U.S. all the way to newly minted world champion Spain. You can also buy gear, including stands for your virtual stadium. It’s a fun element that adds to Kickabout’s replayability as you try to assemble your own World Cup field.

Kickabout has both single-player and dual-player modes, though I found the latter to be a little cramped for my iPhone 17 screen. I imagine head-to-head matches are much more enjoyable on the iPad. Still, Kickabout offers plenty of fun even for single players, as you try to master the game’s different difficulty levels.

Kickabout is free to download, and a $3 in-app purchase gets rid of any ads.

Undolly

The Photos app has a built-in tool to weed out duplicate images, but if you find yourself taking a lot of photos, Undolly brings a whole suite of tools that promise to bring order to your iOS device’s photo library. Besides getting rid of duplicates, the mobile app also lists large videos taking up space in your library, rounds up any screenshots you may have stashed somewhere and keeps tabs on other potential space-takers like RAW, timelapse and animated images.

The value of Undolly will depend heavily on how you use your photo library. For instance, I take a lot of screenshots for articles that I don’t always remember to delete, and the app helped me track down some that were three to five years old. I also appreciate Undolly’s swipable comparisons of similar shots, so you can see for yourself whether the images differ enough to keep.

Undolly’s algorithm also rates images by their framing, quality and expressiveness of subject to better help you determine the shots that deserve a place in your library.

While it’s free to download initially, you will have to subscribe to Undolly to use its features, with a free three-day trial letting you get the lay of the land. After that, a monthly subscription costs $4, while annual and lifetime payments go for $15 and $40, respectively.

VWLSS

Nearly five years after Wordle first appeared, we’re still living in a golden age for daily word puzzles. Add VWLSS and its daily serving of mobile word play to the pile, though there are some unique iPhone elements that could help this free offering earn a place in your regular rotation of gameplay.

You have eight words to guess, each tied to a specific category and with all the vowels stripped out. It’s up to you to figure out the actual word, which you can do either by typing in the answer or using a handy speech feature. I prefer talking to typing, though I’m still sore that my guess of “Bob Barker” in the game show hosts category was misheard as “Bob Parker.” Revenge will be mine tomorrow, I guess.

articles.title: AAPL stock rallies 15% as investors favor AI caution and welcome price increases
articles.subtitle: Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.

While we disagreed with that analysis, investors do now seem to be welcoming the company’s caution when it comes to AI spending, with the stock rallying 15% since that June low …

The company’s shares slid 4% the day after the keynote, but there were a number of macroeconomic factors affecting a wide range of stocks at the same time, including US strikes against Iran after the downing of an American helicopter.

The stock has rallied even more substantially since then, pushing it back into record territory. Bloomberg believes that AI is a factor in this, albeit somewhat indirectly. It suggests that investors are growing increasingly skeptical about AI spending by other companies and says that Apple’s more cautious approach is now seen as a positive.

The stock’s reversal reflects rising unease about the prospects for heavy spending on AI paying off, with Apple’s decision not to participate in the data center arms race increasingly being viewed as an asset, rather than a liability, even though its AI offerings have repeatedly frustrated investors.

“There’s a battle in the market, and right now Apple is benefiting because it isn’t in the storm that the rest of the AI trade is in,” said Mark Bronzo, chief investment strategist at Rye Strategic Partners. “People are concerned about what kind of return hyperscalers could get from their AI spending [and] as a result, investors have gravitated back to Apple as a steady-eddy name without those risks. ”

Louis Navellier, chief investment officer at Navellier & Associates [said] “Pricing for the folding phone will be so strong that it will offset the memory issue on margins, and I think demand will be so strong that it will really support growth.”

While that may prove optimistic, there does seem a clear view that Apple’s financials are headed in the right direction, with expectations of a 17% increase in net income during the current fiscal year.

articles.subtitle: Swing around the map like Spider-Man Jump Links How to get Spider-Man's web shooters in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 3 Spider-Man's web shooters are back in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 3, just in time for the release of Spider-Man: Brand New Day.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Swing around the map like Spider-Man

Jump Links

How to get Spider-Man's web shooters in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 3

Spider-Man's web shooters are back in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 3, just in time for the release of Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

The web shooters are a traversal item where you can become Spider-Man. Shoot it at a tree, building, or pretty much any surface, and you'll swing in its direction. It's an essential mobility item that'll allow you to outrun the storm or speed over to your next location. However, they're not simply found in chests. Instead, you'll need to keep your eye out for other Spider-Man accessories to get them.

Here's how to get Spider-Man's web shooters in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 3.

How to get Spider-Man's web shooters in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 3

You can get Spider-Man's web shooters through two methods:

Purchase it from Spider-Man at The Battlewoods for 2,000 gold bars.

Loot it from a Spider-Man backpack.

Spider-Man will appear at The Battlewoods, but in our experience so far, Spider-Man is not currently in the game. We'll update this guide with his exact location when he appears.

Alternatively, you can loot a Spider-Man backpack, which are backpacks with a spiderweb design that are webbed to walls. They can be found in a bunch of locations all around the map. They'll spawn in the same locations, but they're not guaranteed to spawn every game.

If you're desparately looking to get your hands on a web shooter, we recommend landing at any of the named points of interest, as it seems that each location has at least one backpack spawn. As an example, you can find one on top of the triangular building at Shaken Sanctuary and on the second floor balcony of the building with the Spider-Man mural at The Battlewoods.

articles.title: Always choose the good soap
articles.subtitle: (Angelo D’Amico/Shutterstock) I’ve been thinking about soap again. Back in February I wrote about an Apple-related revelation I had while washing my hands on vacation: We stayed at a nice hotel rather than the less-nice-but-cheaper VRBO condo rental we...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
I’ve been thinking about soap again.

Back in February I wrote about an Apple-related revelation I had while washing my hands on vacation:

We stayed at a nice hotel rather than the less-nice-but-cheaper VRBO condo rental we usually do. Because I’m me, I started thinking about Apple. Like Apple, the nice hotel’s brand promise is that it’s a nice hotel.

If the hotel didn’t clean its rooms well, didn’t provide soap that smelled nice, didn’t maintain the in-room refrigerator, didn’t clean the swimming pool, it would probably decrease its expenses and increase its profit margin. But over time, it would lose its niceness and become a lousy, overpriced hotel.

Earlier this month, John Gruber wrote about how he hopes incoming Apple CEO John Ternus can perform a bit of a reset on Apple’s advertising strategy. In recent months Apple has announced that it’s adding ads to Apple Maps, and ( as John has documented ) it’s allowed incredibly low-quality, scammy ads to infest Apple News.

While Apple can spin adding ads to Apple Maps as a revolutionary new way for businesses to be discovered, it’s telling that its initial announcement was hidden inside a press release about an entirely different product, and introduced as “Enhanced Discoverability in Apple Maps.

” Those choices show that this isn’t something Apple is actually proud of—and that the people in charge of communicating and explaining Apple’s decisions to the world are at odds with those who are making the decisions about expanding revenue.

Apple also recently expanded App Store ads, creating more clutter at the top of App Store search results. It similarly pitched this as an opportunity for developers—but of course, it’s really an opportunity for developers to take a portion of the money they make from the App Store after Apple’s cut and hand it right back to Apple so that their apps don’t become invisible. What a racket.

But Apple’s approach to grinding out additional revenue doesn’t stop with advertising. The recent release of Apple Creator Studio should’ve been a highlight, because it groups a bunch of useful creative apps in one place for a reasonable price. Instead, its launch was marred by the inclusion of Apple’s free productivity apps in the bundle, requiring users to download new versions and (at least initially) display aggressive subscription promotions in the Numbers, Pages, and Keynote interface.

To this day, you’re confronted with an ad for Creator Studio every time you create a new document in those apps, and their default toolbars contain buttons that won’t work unless you subscribe to the bundle.

As a result, Apple has essentially turned its free productivity suite—software that was designed to enhance the inherent value of Apple’s products—into a freemium package with upsell to a creative professional subscription bundle that’s irrelevant (and a terrible value! ) for most of its existing users.

There are many more examples. Using notifications to promote subscriptions and badging the Settings app to push AppleCare plans are among the ways Apple has chosen to intervene in the user experience to drive revenue.

I’m actually not opposed to the idea that Apple should communicate opportunities for its customers to get more out of their devices—but it should be careful not to cross the line into actively annoying those customers. If someone doesn’t want to see what you offer, you need to accept that and go away—not keep needling them. Apple often falls on the wrong side of that line.

Which brings me back to the hotel soap.

Apple’s most valuable asset is its brand. Not its real estate, not its intellectual property, not even any particular product. Even the mighty iPhone has no value if, over time, the traits that differentiate it from competitor products are erased. Apple’s brand has always stood for higher quality products—you pay more, but you get more. Apple has never wanted to be the low-price leader.

It didn’t put stickers on the first Intel Macs to get some marketing dollars from Intel. It doesn’t load up new Macs with loads of lousy bundled third-party software like so many PCs do.

Those are choices Apple has made that cost the company revenue, but they’ve got a bigger purpose. They reinforce the brand.

Opting not to add more revenue to the bottom line is a difficult choice for anyone working at a profit-driven corporation. I used to be in that position at my former employer, defending the overall product against a constant stream of advertising and biz-dev deal proposals that would add incremental revenue. Believe me, arguing to corporate executives that we should leave money on the table is a deeply uncomfortable role to take on—but it’s vital if you care about the bigger picture.

articles.title: Running Simulators Inside Claude Code for Mac
articles.subtitle: Claude Code has a new simulator button. Claude Code’s Mac desktop app has added Apple simulator support, and although it’s billed as “iOS Simulator Support,” it actually works with any iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, or watchOS simulator you have installed.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Claude Code has a new simulator button.

Claude Code’s Mac desktop app has added Apple simulator support, and although it’s billed as “iOS Simulator Support,” it actually works with any iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, or watchOS simulator you have installed.

The process of setting up a simulator is simple. A new button with an iPhone icon appears when you open an existing project. Click it and a new iPhone simulator pane opens to the right by default. However, clicking on the name of the simulator reveals a list of every available simulator. You can also run multiple simulators at once, but that immediately made my aging M1 Max Mac Studio start to chug a little.

With access to your running app, Claude Code is more effective at debugging UI bugs.

Once you have the simulators that you want open, simply ask Claude Code to run and test your app, and it gets to work, building the app, installing it in the simulator, opening it, and poking around. I loaded up a simple word game I’ve been playing with, and after a few minutes, Claude Code found a UI bug while controlling the simulator. I asked it to fix the issue, which it did, then tested and committed. My testing has been limited, but so far it looks like a simple, effective loop.

It’s also worth noting that Claude Code is running the simulator directly inside the Claude app. This is not computer use, meaning windows aren’t going to be opening and getting in your way as you work on something else. All in all, the addition of the simulator, like the inclusion of an in-app sandboxed browser a couple of weeks ago, is a great update to Claude Code.

articles.title: I’m disappointed Apple will charge for AI security camera features in the Home app

articles.content:
iOS 27

One of the things tucked away in the small print of macOS 27 beta 3 is the news that you’ll need a 2TB iCloud+ subscription in order to use the new AI features for home security cameras in the Apple Home app.

While some are suggesting that we shouldn’t be too surprised by this, I do find it a somewhat disappointing move by Apple …

Apple announced significant AI-powered upgrades to the Home app at this year’s WWDC.

Intelligent Home app notifications

One of these was using Apple Intelligence to replace a whole sequence of individual security notifications with a single summary. At present, something as routine as a family member arriving home might generate a notification that they were seen in the driveway, then that the garage door was opened, then that the garage door was closed, then that they were seen at the front door, then that the front door was unlocked, and finally that it was locked.

In iOS 27, all of those individual notifications are replaced with a single one saying that the family member arrived home.

Three AI features for video footage

But the bigger improvements was an upgrade of HomeKit Secure Video from 1080p to 4K, and the use of Apple intelligence to analyze footage from home security cameras. Apple highlighted three intelligent capabilities.

With generated video descriptions, users can quickly understand what happened across a sequence of video clips, even without watching them. They can also search through camera clips so they can easily find what they’re looking for, like a package delivery. At the top of the Search page, the Home app elevates noteworthy clips that users may want to review, so they can quickly see important moments.

articles.title: Wonder Man season 2 canceled by Marvel, report says
articles.subtitle: That's a wrap on Simon Williams Related Four months after Marvel Studios confirmed that Disney Plus series Wonder Man was getting a second season, the company has apparently had a change of heart.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
That's a wrap on Simon Williams

Related

Four months after Marvel Studios confirmed that Disney Plus series Wonder Man was getting a second season, the company has apparently had a change of heart. In yet another sign that everything is getting worse, Disney and Marvel have reportedly opted not to go forward with more Wonder Man, leaving the show's first season's cliffhanger wide open.

Variety reported Thursday, citing sources, that a writers' room for Wonder Man season 2 was never formed and that the show's writers have been released to other projects. That's somewhat ironic, given that Marvel's announcement of a second season of Wonder Man was promoted with what looked like completed scripts for the show's lead characters, Simon Williams and Trevor Slattery.

Series creators Destin Daniel Cretton ( Spider-Man: Brand New Day ) and Andrew Guest ( Community ) were expected to return for the second season, along with series stars Yahya Abdul-Mateen II as struggling superpowered actor Simon Williams and Ben Kingsley as disgraced actor Trevor Slattery (aka The Mandarin), a role Kingsley played across several Marvel projects. According to Variety, Wonder Man 's lead characters could still appear in other Marvel projects in the future.

Wonder Man was a rare season 2 renewal for Marvel Television, which has produced one-and-done shows like The Falcon and The Winter Soldier, Hawkeye, She-Hulk: Attorney at Law, and Ms. Marvel. Only a handful of live-action Marvel Television series like Loki and Daredevil: Born Again have spanned multiple seasons. Wonder Man was released under Marvel's "less homework, more personal stories" Marvel Spotlight banner, but it teed up future stories for Williams and Slattery.

While Wonder Man season 2 is no longer on the table, co-creator Cretton has a lot on his plate. In addition to this week's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Cretton is also developing a live-action adaptation of the beloved manga/anime series Naruto for Lionsgate. It's unclear if Cretton will return for future Tom Holland Spider-Man movies or ever get around to Shang-Chi 2. (That said, the director told Screen Rant this week that a sequel to Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings is "in active development right now.")

Wonder Man debuted on Disney Plus in January. The eight-episode series focuses on Los Angeles actor Simon Williams, a struggling day player with a habit of overthinking the small roles he gets. Oh, and Williams secretly has superpowers. Williams befriends washed-up actor (and former "terrorist") Trevor Slattery as the two fight to land dream roles in the movie Wonder Man.

We gushed over Wonder Man 's blend of humor and subtle superhero action in Polygon's review of the series, calling it "one of the most compelling, purely enjoyable shows in Marvel Studios’ roster. "

Critic Tasha Robinson praised Wonder Man as "the rarest thing in the Marvel playbook: a story that’s unique, personal, character-focused, and designed to stand on its own."

Next up for Marvel Television is VisionQuest, the final part of the saga that started in WandaVision and continued in Agatha All Along. VisionQuest will premiere on Disney Plus in October.

But let's talk about that ending, and the small, important question: Where's Josh Gad?

articles.title: Apple Upgrade makes getting a new Mac easier but not necessarily cheaper
articles.subtitle: Macworld The Apple Upgrade purchase program was introduced earlier this week in the U.S. It’s a leasing program where you agree to a term, pay a monthly fee, and then have to decide what to do with the device you bought at the end of the term.
articles.author: Macworld
articles.content:
The Apple Upgrade purchase program was introduced earlier this week in the U.S. It’s a leasing program where you agree to a term, pay a monthly fee, and then have to decide what to do with the device you bought at the end of the term. If you are familiar with car leases, Apple Upgrade will make perfect sense.

When you’re in a situation where you need to buy a new Mac, it’s nice to have purchasing options that suit your finances. But regardless of how you buy a Mac, you should understand the implications of how you pay for your Mac. Sometimes, it’s pretty straightforward, but other times, it’s a little more involved.

Apple Upgrade is one of those times when it’s a little more involved. Let’s take a look at what you’re getting into if you enroll in Apple Upgrade. This can help you decide if it’s a plan that suits your needs, or if you should pay a different way.

Apple Upgrade: What I’m buying

In this examination, I’ll be looking at what’s involved with buying a 14-inch MacBook Pro. Apple Upgrade will appeal to customers in the market for pricier Mac models, so with that in mind, these are the specs of the MacBook Pro I’ll use for this article.

The price of this laptop as configured is $2,649 without AppleCare+. Apple Upgrade does not include AppleCare coverage, and I won’t be including it in the analysis. Sales tax and other fees are also not calculated here.

Apple Upgrade: Terms and cost

For this particular MacBook Pro, Apple offers two Apple Upgrade term options:

24-months: $74.34 per month. After 24 months, the total payment equals $1,784.16 (67 percent of the total $2,649).

36-months: $52.87 per month. After 36 months, the total payment equals $1,903.32 (72 percent of the total $2,649).

Apple Upgrade looks appealing: The monthly fees are a lot more manageable than paying full price for an outright purchase or even financing it through the Apple Card, which would cost $220.75 per month for a year. The total amount you have spent when the term ends seems attractive, too.

With leases such as Apple Upgrade, the true value–or lack of it–comes when the terms end, and you have to decide what you are going to do with the Mac. Apple Upgrade gives you three options; let’s take a look.

At the end of the Apple Upgrade lease, Apple offers three options for your next step.

Foundry

End of lease: Buy the Mac

You can decide to buy the Mac after you’ve made all 24 or 36 payments. The fees you’ve paid count towards the original purchase price; you then pay the remaining cost in one sum. In our example, the price would be:

$864.84 when the 24-month term ends

$745.68 when the 36-month term ends

articles.title: macOS 27 Golden Gate: The MacStories Public Beta Preview
articles.subtitle: The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.

It’s not my final take on Golden Gate by any means; after all, I’ve only been using it for about a month, and there will be several more turns in the beta cycle between now and the public release. However, I’ve used Golden Gate long enough to help you make an informed decision about whether or not to install the public beta now.

Of course, it’s impossible for me to account for everyone’s unique Mac setups when considering Golden Gate’s stability, but it’s worth reiterating what I’ve said in past previews: modern Apple betas have been consistently stable. That’s to say, the risks of using the public beta are modest. It’s been years since I’ve had a critical app fail or lost data.

I never go into beta season without a backup plan, though. If something goes terribly wrong, I have backups, backups of those backups, and alternate Macs I can switch to in the event of a disaster. I don’t expect to have to go to Plan B, but if you’re going to jump on the Beta Bus, you should have a Plan B, too.

Okay, you’ve been warned. Let’s get to the fun part.

Supported By

Inoreader

Every year’s macOS update is a little different, but Golden Gate is more different than most. Instead of focusing on tentpole features and apps (with the exception of a new Siri app), macOS 27’s updates fall into three broad categories:

refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design language,

hundreds of system-level changes intended to improve your Mac’s performance, and

Apple Intelligence, which includes the new Siri app as well as many other AI additions to existing system apps.

It’s been a while since the “Snow Leopard Moment.”

With so many past macOS updates focusing on system apps, it’s refreshing to see Apple take a more holistic system-level approach, which harkens back to how most people remember OS X Snow Leopard. In fact, during WWDC briefings, Apple representatives likened the Golden Gate update to Snow Leopard before anyone in the room even asked about it.

Snow Leopard is remembered as a release that focused on performance over features. The reality is that the update also introduced its fair share of new features, but many were less splashy from a user-facing standpoint. They were under-the-hood updates that made the Mac work better without users having to think about it much. In that sense, Golden Gate has a lot in common with Snow Leopard.

Other than the brand new Siri app, you probably won’t notice that much is different when you first launch the new version. But over time, the changes will reveal themselves, adding up to a whole that – with few exceptions – is greater than the parts.

So let’s take a closer look at how Liquid Glass has evolved, the most significant system changes, and what it’s like to use Siri and other Apple Intelligence updates in Golden Gate’s public beta.

Design

Windows stand out from each other more, and the sidebar runs edge to edge in Golden Gate.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

As a former delivery guy, I have a fondness in my heart for videogame trucking. It lets me reclaim the simple satisfaction of moving things where they need to go without needing to endure all the things that make people glad they aren't a delivery guy. There's just one problem: Videogame truckin' isn't weird enough.

My six years of delivery work regularly involved surreal events, uncanny individuals, inexplicable decisions, and plenty of other inscrutable encounters. Videogame trucking, however, tends to be extremely scrutable—until this week, when developer Code Wakers launched an open playtest for Prospice: Anomalous Logistics, an upcoming driving and delivery sim that's properly unfathomable.

In Prospice, you play as an employee of an organization that would be right at home alongside the SCP Foundation, the Federal Bureau of Control, and any number of groups poking around the Backrooms. Its mission is researching an island that is, in the Steam description's words, "cursed by the corpses of ever rotting gods" and "a place where the world itself unravels."

Unfortunately, the open wilderness isn't the best environment for researching the remains of a massive, mouldering entity—which is where you come in. As a logistics driver, you'll undertake delivery tasks to support and supply the expedition, all while managing fuel, navigating unpaved terrain, and ensuring whatever still-twitching godflesh might be weighing down your flatbed gets to its destination unspoiled. Ideally while surviving, which—in my experience—isn't guaranteed.

When I started the playtest, I was just yards away from a massive, partially unearthed corpse, its hand already removed and waiting in my truck for transport—cargo that was, I'll admit, somewhat eerier than anything I've delivered in person. But still, despite how much that severed hell-hand continually quivered throughout the drive, I completed my inaugural delivery with only some passing clumsiness as I juggled gears to get my truck over and through some swamp mud and rocky inclines.

articles.title: Unlock or recover your Mac using a special boot volume
articles.subtitle: Several years ago, Apple began hiding disk partitions and volumes on the startup drive. The first was a secret volume with a tiny operating system on it that would let you boot from it, after which you could restore from a Time Machine backup, run First Aid...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Several years ago, Apple began hiding disk partitions and volumes on the startup drive. The first was a secret volume with a tiny operating system on it that would let you boot from it, after which you could restore from a Time Machine backup, run First Aid in Disk Utility, or reinstall Mac OS X or macOS. Over the years, Apple has multiplied those hidden locations and added more sophistication to what they offer.

These boot volumes are:

recoveryOS: The current name and form of the special volume described above, which boots into the Recovery Assistant “app. ” You can run Disk Utility (and First Aid), reinstall macOS, launch Safari to access Apple Support pages, modify startup security settings (rarely required these days), and access Terminal. With Terminal, you can reset your macOS password.

If your Mac can’t start up properly, it will try to launch the Recovery process within recoveryOS, which performs automatic repairs that Apple doesn’t document. If successful, you can then restart into macOS.

Fallback recoveryOS: If recoveryOS is damaged—and that can happen—you can press the power button twice, quickly, and then keep holding it the second time. This fallback recovery volume can’t change startup security, but it can help you diagnose what’s going on. This is the duct-tape belt that helps if your pants come unbuttoned (macOS won’t boot) and your suspenders break (regular recoveryOS fails).

Repair Assistant: From a powered-down state, press the power button until you hear the startup chime, then press and hold Command-D. (On an Intel Mac, hold the D key at startup. ) The Diagnostics app can run hardware tests that might help narrow down a problem before you bring in Apple Support, or they may ask you to boot into that mode and share the results of the tests they have you run.

Repair Assistant can fail, too, if its volume is damaged. You may then have to perform a special “ revive or restore ” operation, which requires another Mac. Or you may need a full reinstall using a bootable macOS installer.

macOS: macOS is a sort of hidden boot volume for the last several releases. You don’t boot from the system; instead, a read-only snapshot of the system is mounted, and then booted from. This is part of Apple making system resources immutable through cryptography and at startup.

Besides using recoveryOS for the above tasks, you might also need to use it to unlock your Mac after locking it in Find My and to reset your password using a FileVault Recovery Key. Here’s how.

Unlock your Mac

While it’s not a common scenario, it could happen to you: you accidentally leave your Mac somewhere, or it’s stolen. Thinking quickly, you launch Find My on another of your devices or go to iCloud. com/find and log in. You then tap or click a few buttons to lock your Mac. If the Mac is connected to the Internet, it restarts and locks immediately.

(Despite promising to display the message you entered when you locked it, macOS does not do so. ) If it’s not connected, it restarts the next time it has Internet access.

The account used to lock the Mac is the only one that can unlock it, and you must be in front of the Mac to perform that operation. Apple limits each Mac to having Find My enabled from a single account. Here are the steps:

When you see the macOS Recovery title, click the account profile below it. Enter the account’s password and click Continue.

If you entered it correctly, “Authentication succeeded” appears. Click Restart.

The Mac restarts and shows Activate Mac after it boots up. This time, all the active macOS accounts are shown. Click one, and then enter its password. Click Next.

You now can choose to either use your Apple Account or a macOS password to continue. If you opt for the Apple Account, enter the full address or phone number as shown. Then enter the account’s password. Otherwise, you can click to enter the Mac password, which Apple says is the last one used to unlock the Mac in a regular session before it was locked.

If you’re the only user on the Mac, that’s easy to figure out. (In testing with Golden Gate public beta 2, I wasn’t able to get the Mac password option to work, and I’ve had it fail in Tahoe, too. ) Sometimes neither works. Choose Restart from the Apple menu in that case and try again.

articles.title: Finishing with Fable 5
articles.subtitle: When Fable 5 returned last week, I knew exactly what to throw at it. In February, I started a project out of frustration that likewise ended in frustration, so I put it on the shelf and waited.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
When Fable 5 returned last week, I knew exactly what to throw at it. In February, I started a project out of frustration that likewise ended in frustration, so I put it on the shelf and waited. Five months later, Fable 5 was released, and I knew it was time to finish Editor, a single-view diffing tool for writers rather than developers.

At MacStories, we all write in Markdown, and we’ve used GitHub to share and sync changes among team members since 2015. GitHub is primarily a developer tool, but it’s a fast, reliable way to share our Markdown-formatted article files, too.

We use GitHub the most for the Club MacStories newsletters. Every week, Federico, Devon, Jonathan, and I work on sections for MacStories Weekly and save them to a GitHub repo. That allows any of us to sync the sections locally for reading, editing, and assembling the issue.

The trouble is that as great as Markdown text editors are to write and GitHub is for versioning and syncing, there isn’t a good way to view the changes someone has made to a document. I know because I’ve been looking for a solution for a long time. Some Markdown apps like iA Writer and Bear support versioning or backups, but I’ve yet to find a text editor that can visualize changes made by someone else based on a document’s Git history.

Of course, developers have many ways to track changes to code, including GitHub Desktop, Kaleidoscope, and Git Tower. Code is just text, so those apps can be used by writers, too. However, the process of writing and editing prose is fundamentally different from code. I’ve tried the apps above and others, and it’s just too hard to track changes in the formats development tools use.

This is what it’s like trying to track changes in GitHub Desktop.

We wouldn’t have stuck with GitHub as long as we have if it didn’t work, but that hasn’t made the friction of reviewing changes any less frustrating, especially on Fridays when we send MacStories Weekly. That’s when I had the idea for Editor. I was trying to parse some changes Devon had made to one of my stories with GitHub Desktop, and the friction finally got to me.

One obvious problem was the side-by-side document view many code diffing tools use. I wanted more detail than most diffing tools offer, but in a single, readable view, so I could skim through changes quickly.

Most agent-assisted projects benefit from some up-front research and planning. I knew what I wanted would sink or swim on the design, not the app’s underlying Markdown viewer, so I spent time researching systems for visualizing document edits.

That’s when I came across Upwelling, a multi-author project from Ink & Switch that describes itself as “an independent research lab exploring the future of tools for thought.” In their research paper, the authors described my exact problem:

Unfortunately, version control tools like Git, which are designed for software development, do not suit the needs of writers. Git cannot compare or merge files from WYSIWYG editors such as Microsoft Word… and graphical user interfaces for Git are cluttered with complex concepts such as commit hashes and visualizations of non-linear branching and merging histories.

Ink & Switch’s solution, a prototype collaborative text editor, wasn’t what I wanted to build, but the research behind it was full of interesting ideas that helped me settle on several principles for what would become Editor:

Document changes needed to be visible in a single view that carefully balanced highlighting changes with readability;

A writer should be able to instantly switch from the marked-up version of their document to the clean original and edited final version;

Changes needed to be categorized by filterable types like punctuation, word choice, capitalization, insertions, and deletions to reduce clutter in heavily edited documents;

Change types would be color coded using a side rail system inspired by maps of London’s tube system;

Navigating among individual edits needed to be done by simple j/k keyboard input; and

Global document navigation should employ a mini-map of a document’s edit regions (a feature borrowed from developer IDEs like Xcode) to make it easy to jump from one area of a document to another.

Live session held at the Steve Jobs Theater during WWDC26 now available

The Apple Developer YouTube channel shared an interesting 90-minute WWDC26 session today called “ Inside Apple Intelligence and Xcode: Special Presentation. ”

The result is a WWDC badge tracker app featuring 3D animations, holographic effects, and even Visual Intelligence capabilities—all created from just a few prompts.

Along the way, the demo highlights new Xcode 27 features that come into play before coding begins, including asking clarifying and follow-up questions and mapping out the project in advance.

The session continues with demos and valuable information on how apps can integrate with the new Siri AI, how developers can leverage the new Apple Foundation Models framework, and, in turn, how the framework integrates with the new Core AI framework and the upgraded MLX framework, even when using third-party models.

The special presentation ends with an impressive demo of the 1-trillion-parameter Kimi 2.6 model running locally in LM Studio across four Mac Studios, using the low-latency RDMA-over-Thunderbolt technology Apple introduced with macOS Tahoe 26.2.

articles.title: Director Of New Soulslike Says ‘No AI Used In The Final Game’ After Big YouTubers Sounded The Alarm Over A Recent Preview Build
articles.subtitle: AI Soulslike Steam The Relic: First Guardian The Relic: First Guardian, the upcoming Soulslike from developer Project Cloud Games and publisher Perp Games that’s set to release on July 31, immediately drew criticism from several content creators for its...
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
AI Soulslike Steam The Relic: First Guardian

The Relic: First Guardian, the upcoming Soulslike from developer Project Cloud Games and publisher Perp Games that’s set to release on July 31, immediately drew criticism from several content creators for its suspected use of AI-generated assets during the previews that went out towards the end of last month. The director has now responded to those critiques, stating that AI was only used early on and that, while minor AI elements may be in the demo build folks have played, none will be in the final game.

If you’ve not heard of The Relic: First Guardian, that’s certainly not due to the publisher’s lack of advertising. Trailers for the game have been published on the YouTube accounts of both PlayStation and IGN, and Perp Games has been giving demo build keys to basically any content creator even vaguely associated with the Soulslike genre. It seems to have worked too, as the publishers recently announced that The Relic: First Guardian has been wishlisted over 250,000 times across both Steam and PlayStation 5.

Indeed, I was only reminded of this game’s existence after watching Iron Pineapple’s recent video featuring it and—look, I know they say “all press is good press,” but Iron Pineapple was one of many content creators, alongside the likes of FightinCowboy, who suggested that The Relic: First Guardian’s preview build looked a little off. Artwork, item icons, text, dialogue—all of it came off as suspicious.

The game’s director, In-Hyeok Park, was recently asked about the presence of AI-generated content in The Relic: First Guardian during an interview with Thumb Wars, and he confirmed that “one or two elements” of AI-gen’d content “may” have made it into the preview build. However, he seems pretty certain that none of the aforementioned slop is going to make its way into the final game.

“There is no AI used in the final game; however, in the early design stages, AI was used in a very few areas to help in the concept stage of development. This involved a few pieces of concept art for loading screens and a handful of icon images for the consumables,” stated Park.

“Although there may be one or two elements of this AI still in the preview build, the final product will not have any of this AI work in the game,” he continued. “AI was also used in the early stage to help localize text, although all text was then manually reviewed and edited by Project Cloud Staff and no AI was used in the game’s voiceovers.”

It’s possible any generative AI work was removed from the final version of the game, or content creators were seeing signs of slop that was never there to begin with. The game’s Steam page has no AI disclosure.

At least one early review dinged the game for its use of AI voice overs for quest givers, though it didn’t take issue with any of the rest of the game appearing to hinge on the work of generative AI tools. “Truly, no voice at all would’ve been better than the robotic garbage I experienced,” RPGFan wrote.

articles.title: Review: Xteink X3 is the little e-reader the world’s not quite ready for
articles.subtitle: An e-reader magneted to the back of a smartphone, just as the prophecy foretold. The market for small e-readers has been booming lately.
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
The market for small e-readers has been booming lately. Earlier this year, Jason took a look at the Xteink X4, a pint-sized reading device that was about as light and small as they come. But those maniacs at Xteink weren’t done yet: they followed it up with the $79 X3, which is unbelievably even lighter and smaller.

I wouldn’t blame you for wondering if there’s such a thing as too small and light—at 3.84 inches by 2.51 inches (and just 0.2 inches thick) the X3 is still larger than, say, a credit card, but not by much. The screen itself measures just 3.7 inches, more than half an inch smaller than the X4’s 4.3 inch, but its 259 ppi resolution still makes it plenty easy to read on. 1 At that size it’s little imposition to take it with you wherever you go. Easy to lose? Maybe. Easy to love? Yes.

For one thing, this small size unlocks at least one capability that the X4 couldn’t fully deliver upon—the ability to stick to the back of your phone. Like the X4, the X3 has a MagSafe-compatible magnet in its rear case and it fits just about perfectly on the back of my iPhone 17 Pro, nestled below the camera plateau.

However, the magnet is not particularly strong, and it lacks the secondary stabilizing magnet that you see on official MagSafe accessories, meaning it wobbles around a bit. I wouldn’t call it a super secure connection, but it’s pretty good if you’re just slipping it in and out of a pocket. Just be aware that it probably will come loose.

Like the X4 before it, the X3 features a pair of rocker switches on the front for a total of four possible buttons. But they’ve opted to skip the X4’s side mounted rocker switch in favor of a single buttons on each side. There’s also an on/off switch at the top (plus a recessed button used for resetting the device). And with all of that, they somehow managed to continue to fit a microSD slot in the top. The bottom left corner also has a little set of holes for a lanyard or wrist strap.

The one casualty of the smaller X3, however, is the port. The X4 was big enough to accommodate a USB-C connector, but the X3’s thin profile makes that impossible. Instead, there’s a pogo-pin USB cable that connects to four magnetic contacts on the reader. Is this a step back? Strictly speaking, yes.

Using a proprietary connector is a bummer in the year 2026, especially because it means having to keep track of a single-use cable. That said, once you get the X3 up and running, the only real need for the connector is charging, and the battery on this thing lasts a very long time. (I’ve yet to run it down in several weeks of usage.

) Just remember to make a note of where you stow that cable for the point months down the road when you do need to charge it and find yourself wondering whatever happened to it.

As with the X4, the X3 lacks any sort of screen lighting, meaning that it’s strictly a “read in bright light” device. But don’t worry, because Xteink has already unveiled a new X4 Pro with the company’s first lit screen. 2

All in all, I found the X3 very comfortable to read on, whether attached to my iPhone or not. The side buttons work great as page-turners, and the screen is high-contrast and sharp enough to make text render very clearly. All in all, it’s a great reading experience—if you take into account one major caveat.

Soft where?

The elephant in the room for the Xteink X3 is the software. Xteink ships the X3 with its own built-in firmware which, by all accounts, has improved since the first version. But I can’t really tell you, because upon opening the box and powering up the device, the first thing I did was install Crosspoint, the open-source community-built firmware that has turned this device from a curiosity into a real contender. 3

Unlike a lot of other firmware replacements, Crosspoint is super easy to install; you can do it right from a web browser. While it’s not fully free of technological hurdles, I’d say that most people comfortable using an e-reader or updating their iPhones will be able to handle the process with few problems. And the benefits are manifold.

Crosspoint goes beyond simply turning this into a functional device and into one that is actually fun to use. It’s got a straightforward, easy to navigate interface that makes it simple to do everything from reading to loading books (accomplished via a web-based interface). For those who like to tweak their reading setup, there are plenty of configuration options, everything from screen orientation to hyphenation and, yes, custom fonts loaded via the SD card.

Even the onscreen keyboard that you need to use for various configuration tasks is pretty solid for what’s available—on par with navigating via an onscreen keyboard with a game controller, in my opinion. I wouldn’t want to have to type in my Wi-Fi password every time—and you don’t, because it saves it for you—but one time was fine.

There are also a bunch of other features that might appeal to those who want to take reading to the next level. For example, support for Open Publication Distribution System (OPDS) standard means that if you want to host your book library on your own server, you can point your reader at that and download any of the books you already own directly to your device. There’s also support for KOreader sync to help keep your place between supported devices. 4

Crosspoint has been so successful, in fact, that the team at Xteink has smartened up and started collaborating. (This after a brief moment when it looked like the company might try to firmware lock its devices.

) Now, not only do the “developer editions” sold directly by the company continue to allow you to install the custom firmware, the company has been working with the Crosspoint team to make sure new devices, like the X4 Pro, will already be supported when they arrive. While Xteink hasn’t quite adopted Crosspoint as the default OS, it’s not far off.

Over at Snazzy Labs, Quinn Nelson has a great in-depth look at the changes coming to Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit with macOS 27 this fall. Paired with Metal 4, it’s a real leap over what’s possible today, and Nelson showcases the difference well.

Thanks to the upcoming update, Nelson was able to use CrossOver, a Windows-to-Mac compatibility layer that allows PC games to be played on a Mac, to spotlight some impressive numbers on games ranging from Red Dead Redemption to the recently released 007 First Light.

Not all games Nelson tried showed the same leap in performance, but that’s true on compatibility layers like Proton on the Steam Deck, too. Nelson also makes a pitch for an Apple gaming device. I agree with him that more than ever, the pieces, right down to a hardware-focused incoming CEO, are all there for such a device, and I remain optimistic. articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation. articles.title: Machine Party, out now, is masochistic Mario Party from the dev that brought you Buckshot Roulette
articles.subtitle: Let's a go! There is an obvious humour to be found in the contrast between the visual presentation of Mario Party and the agita and unbridled rage it brings out in people. This is not a game about violence, yet it pulls it out from people nonetheless.
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
Let's a go!

There is an obvious humour to be found in the contrast between the visual presentation of Mario Party and the agita and unbridled rage it brings out in people. This is not a game about violence, yet it pulls it out from people nonetheless. So, how about something that leans into this violence, while still retaining the jovially competitive nature? Enter Machine Party, the latest from Buckshot Roulette developer Mike Klubnika, made alongside GDeavid, a party game "where failure is lethal."

Machine Party truly is masochistic Mario Party. You need at least two people to play, and it can run up to four people, with however many of you there are forced into brutal, lawless minigames where you desperately want to be the person that finishes first otherwise your death is likely imminent. There are a bevy of games to play through, all of which just teeter over the edge of silliness that would allow them to be found in the Saw franchise.

One game sees you running around a room in hopes of not being shredded to bits by a roomba with a buzz saw attached to it. Another places a brutalist Rubik's Cube in front of you that you have to destroy square by square in order to match a particular shape. Fail to do so, and your brains are on the walls. A third sees you eating as many peas, one a time, as fast as you can.

Do the worst, that's right, brains on the walls again. And we find ourselves back to being shredded in a fourth (but not final, there appear to be a good few) minigame which sees you attempting to run up an escalator that's going down, a pit of sawblades at its bottom.

Every inch of the game is as ridiculous as it is gorey, which I'm sure will delight enough of you out there. As it stands, it should be noted, there is no local co-op. A launch day Steam post clarifies that this will be coming in late August, explaining that there were no plans for it originally, but enough folks asked for it so it's happening.

articles.title: Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Fans Are Really Curious What A Change In The Remake’s ESRB Rating Means
articles.subtitle: ESRB Nintendo Remake Switch 2 The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Last month, Nintendo announced the previously rumored Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake with a very short teaser.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
ESRB Nintendo Remake Switch 2 The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

Last month, Nintendo announced the previously rumored Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake with a very short teaser. We still basically know nothing about what the remake actually is or when it will release later this year. But a new ESRB rating for the game already has fans wondering if the classic Nintendo 64 game might be making an unexpected change to its Great Fairies.

On July 29, Nintendo quietly updated the official store page for the upcoming Ocarina of Time remake. The page now features an ESRB rating of E10+ and lists some of the content that earned the remake this rating. According to the store page, this Zelda remake includes “Animated Blood, Fantasy Violence.” Not surprising, considering the original game and the 3DS remaster both featured swords, combat, and killing.

But this remake’s ESRB rating is missing something. The 3DS remaster of Ocarina of Time is also rated E10, but mentions “Animated Blood, Fantasy Violence, and Suggestive Themes. ” The original Ocarina of Time was simply rated E, but that doesn’t mean much, as the E10 rating didn’t exist when the original game shipped on N64 back in 1998.

This has some fans worried that Nintendo might be making changes to the remake. Many think the original game’s fairies might get redesigned. The original designs might look a bit too sexy for Nintendo’s liking in a more modern, realistic art style.

This isn’t too outlandish of a theory. If you look up the ESRB rating description for the Ocarina of Time 3DS remaster, you can find this section that seems to indicate the fairies are partially to blame for the added suggestive themes warning:

Link encounters a few female characters that are depicted from low camera angles and dressed in outfits that display moderate amounts of cleavage

Others have suggested certain areas or lines might get tweaked to make them a bit less dark or adult. However, something to keep in mind is that when Ocarina of Time was re-released via Virtual Console on the Wii, it was rated E by the ESRB, didn’t include a suggestive themes warning, and as far as I can tell, the fairies weren’t altered at all in that version of the classic game.

And let’s not forget what the fairies looked like in Breath of the Wild. Those ladies were big, didn’t wear much, and have inspired plenty of raunchy fan art. So perhaps Ocarina’s fairies will look more like that, which I think a lot of fans would love.

Perhaps people are worried about nothing. Or maybe the fairies really will be more covered up or redesigned entirely. For now, we can only speculate until we see more of the game, which is set to arrive on Switch 2 sometime later this year.
